Natalia: Sir, I think we need to review some things before the exam begins.
Instructor: I agree; you may consider historical information is not important for this job, but it is! If you know the history behind a simple concept like data warehousing, the concept itself becomes clearer and easier to understand.
Natalia: Yes! Please, give us a summary of the history of data warehousing, for I don't remember much of it.

Instructor: OK, let's go back to the 1980's, databases are not very sophisticated, and engineers are about to discover a big problem: if they optimize the database for transactions, it is not efficient for reporting and data analysis purposes; so, integration with decision support systems becomes very complicated. Two people realize about this problem and come up with a solution: Data warehousing. They are Bill Inmon and Ralph Kimball; the first one coins the term "Data Warehouse" in the 70's. Do you understand the problem they found, and their solution?
Natalia: I may be wrong, but let's see: if I have a database that I use for transactions, it’s difficult to use the data in it to create reports unless I use a relational model.
Instructor: Exactly. And that relational model is part of the solution popularized in the 1990's with data warehousing applications. In general, the concept of data warehousing refers to saving all data from different sources in a single storage location, until we need to use it. Is that clear?

Natalia: Let's see…If we store all information from our data sources in a single tool, can we use it all at once?
Instructor: Correct! In 1992, Inmon writes a book called “Building the Data Warehouse”, and Kimball publishes “The Data Warehouse Toolkit” in 1996. These two books offer different approaches to relational modeling, yet they are equally good at explaining how to implement data warehousing in business environments.
Natalia: I'm sorry, sir; I'm going to write down the titles of the books while you finish your explanation.

• Zero conditional for describing the main features of data warehousing

Read your paragraph aloud to a partner.

As you should know already, the general purpose of conditionals is expressing cause-effect or action-consequence relationships.

In the case of the Zero conditional, the effect or consequence expressed is considered a truth or a fact. This is the reason we use Present Simple in the two clauses that make up this conditional structure:

• If we don't implement a data warehouse in the company,the company doesn't keep track of its data.
• When you implement a data warehouse, you keep all your data into one tool.

The examples above show the basic negative and affirmative structures, respectively. You can also see, from the second example, that the word when can replace the word if in a conditional sentence. Also, notice the comma that separates the two sentences of the conditional. This comma is always necessary when the if sentence goes first. But remember, you can also start with the consequence, and in this case, we do not use the comma: 

• The company doesn't keep track of its data if we don't implement a data warehouse in the company,
• you keep all your data into one tool when you implement a data warehouse.

We can also use the zero conditional in interrogative form to ask about the consequence of an action when we have an assumption of what the consequence is. Let's compare the following questions:

• What happens if we update the database?
• Does performance improve if we update the database?

In the first one, we are not suggesting any possible consequence, and that is evident by the use of what. In the second one, we're using an interrogative phrase in Present Simple (Does performance improve) to express our assumption.

Something else to notice: The answer to the first question must be an open-ended one, and the answer to the second will probably be a yes/no answer.

We can classify conjunctions into two categories depending on the type of clauses they connect. Knowing this will help you improve your writing.

You probably know this already: a conjunction is a word that connects two ideas in a sentence. Now, depending on the type of relationship that these ideas have, we will connect them using coordinating or subordinating conjunctions. But, what's the difference? Let's take a look at the following example:

• This software is expensive but its features make it the best!

As you can see, there are two independent parts of this sentence, and they are joined by the conjunction but. The difference between these two types of conjunctions is that coordinating conjunctions join two independent clauses, and subordinating conjunctions join an independent clause with a subordinate one. We will explain this later, but first, let's take a look at the list of conjunctions, so you can memorize them; look for their definition and share them with your peers:
Please, give us a summary of the history of data warehousing, for I don't remember much of it.
These two books offer different approaches to relational modeling, yet they are equally good at explaining how to implement data warehousing
Save all data from different sources in a single storage location, until we need to use it.

Now that you know the conjunctions, you need to understand what dependent and independent clauses are.

An independent clause is a phrase with three characteristics: it has a subject, it contains an action (or predicate), and it expresses a full idea; this means that an independent clause works as a sentence. Let's see some examples:

• I want to implement a database.
• Jane is reading a manual.
• I work.
• Cleanse the database.

The examples above are all independent clauses; they don't need additional information to express a complete idea. Now, a subordinate clause is a phrase that does not express a complete idea; this may be because there is no subject, or there is no action, or something is missing. Let's see some examples:

• When I switch the software.
• For she has to implement the new software.
• While you are working there.
• Until it looks perfect.

These phrases are dependent because they do not express a full idea; we are missing some information (What happens when you switch the software?
What happens while you are working there?). Let's see the two groups of examples joined together:

• I want to implement a database when I switch the software.
• Cleanse the database until it looks perfect.
• Jane is reading a manual for she has to implement the new software.


Now, both parts of each sentence make sense! The dependent clauses are working as the complement of the independent ones. The main idea of the sentence is always located in an independent clause, while the information that the subordinate clauses provide is additional, but not necessary for the sentence to make sense.
Now, let's see some examples of two clauses joined by coordinating conjunctions:

• I updated this database and all the information was erased!
• This computer is old but you can open database sheets in it.
• I don't like this keyboard, so I bought a new one.

In the examples above, the first and second parts of each sentence express a full idea; there is not emphasis in one of the two parts because the two are equally important fort the meaning of the sentence.

To conclude this review: Use coordinating conjunctions when you want to express two complete ideas, and use subordinating conjunctions when you want to provide additional information to complement the main idea of an independent clause.

A timeline is a sequence of events organized in a chronological way. Sequencing such events will help you remember the information in a better way, and it'll provide a big picture on how something, such as an invention, has evolved.

Let's suppose you're going to write a timeline on the history of data warehousing; bear these tips in mind:

1. Read texts on the topic and take notes related to the most important events.
2. Make a list with all the dates and organize them chronologically (from the earliest event to the latest one).
3.Think about how you're going to divide your timeline (days, months, years or centuries).
4. Draw a line and place each event on your list.
5. It's a good idea to create conventions (as color conventions) for you and the potential reader of the timeline to have information clear. For example: use red for events that are related to “The Data Warehouse Toolkit.”
